paragraphs.text: MUHAMMAD JAWAD ZAFAR, J.: Through the instant petition under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan (“Constitution”), the petitioner has called in question the order dated 04.02.2026 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge/Ex-Officio Justice of the Peace, Faisalabad, whereby his petition seeking compliance with the earlier order dated 11.10.2025 was disposed of. As a consequence, he seeks a direction to the Federal Investigation Agency (“FIA”) to register a criminal case against the respondent no.6 and others on the strength of Medico Legal Examination Certificate No. 140/2025.

The facts, shorn of unnecessary detail, lie in a narrow compass. The petitioner moved a petition under Sections 22-A and 22-B of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (“Cr.P.C.”) before the learned Ex- Officio Justice of the Peace, Faisalabad, seeking a direction to the SHO, FIA Composite Circle, Faisalabad, to register a criminal case against the respondent no.6 and others. He alleged that on 08.05.2024 his real brother, Naeem alias Noni, was abducted from the main road near the Women College, Madina Town, Faisalabad, within the territorial limits of Police Station Madina Town, by officials of CIA City, Faisalabad, acting under the command of Inspector Sadiq Cheema, the then In- charge, CIA. According to him, his brother was thereafter illegally Date of hearing: 30.10.2026 Petitioner by: Mr. Nadeem Shibli, Advocate. State by: Mr. Faisal Abbas Ranjha, Assistant Attorney General for Pakistan. Respondent No.7 by: Rana Sarfraz Ahmad Khan, Advocate. confined at various places, including torture cells said to be maintained by the police, and was subjected to severe torture. On an application moved for the purpose, he was medically examined on the direction of the learned Area Magistrate. The learned Ex-Officio Justice of the Peace called for a report from the FIA, which disclosed that the petitioner had appeared on 09.10.2025 and produced his evidence, and that the matter stood registered as Inquiry No. 1642/2025. By order dated 11.10.2025, the petition was disposed of with a direction to the FIA to conclude the inquiry on merits within thirty days. That order was never assailed. The petitioner thereafter sought its compliance, whereupon the FIA reported that the inquiry had been dropped by the Director, FIA, Faisalabad. Finding that the earlier order stood complied with, the learned Ex- Officio Justice of the Peace disposed of the compliance petition through the impugned order dated 04.02.2026. Hence, this petition.

Learned counsel for the petitioner, with considerable vehemence, contends that the application for registration of a case disclosed cognizable offences of abduction, illegal confinement and custodial torture, fortified by the Medico Legal Examination Certificate of the petitioner’s brother, and that the learned Ex-Officio Justice of the Peace ought to have directed the registration of a case rather than relegating the matter to an inquiry. He submits that the inquiry was dropped by the Director, FIA, Faisalabad without any reasoned finding, and that the compliance petition was disposed of mechanically, without examining whether the inquiry had in truth been concluded on merits as directed. Per contra, the learned Law Officer opposes the petition tooth and nail. He contends that the order dated 11.10.2025 was never challenged and has attained finality, that the FIA conducted the inquiry after the petitioner had appeared and produced his evidence, and that the matter was dropped by the competent authority. In his submission, the compliance petition could only examine whether that order had been obeyed, and the learned Ex-Officio rightly found that it had. He adds that the petitioner cannot, under the garb of compliance proceedings, re-agitate the merits of his original petition, and that he remains at liberty to file a private complaint, if so advised.

Having given anxious consideration to the rival contentions, two questions emerge for determination. The first is whether the impugned order, passed in proceedings for compliance of the order dated 11.10.2025, is tainted by any illegality or jurisdictional defect. The second is whether, independently of that order, a writ in the nature of mandamus can be issued directing the FIA to register a criminal case against the respondent no.6 and others. Since the second question turns on the nature of the writ and the statutory duties of the FIA, it is convenient first to notice the governing principles and the statutory scheme, and then to answer both questions in turn.

Mandamus is a prerogative writ of ancient lineage, by which a superior court commands a public authority to perform a public duty cast upon it by law. Under our constitutional dispensation, the jurisdiction is anchored in Article 199(1)(a)(i) of the Constitution, which empowers this Court, on the application of an aggrieved party, to direct a person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Federation, a Province or a local authority “to do anything he is required by law to do”. The words “required by law” are the key to the remedy. The writ presupposes a legal duty owed to the petitioner and a corresponding legal right vested in him, and where either is absent the writ cannot be issued. It was for this reason that the Honourable Supreme Court of Pakistan, in “Secretary Finance and others v. Ghulam Safdar”1 , set aside a writ of mandamus, finding that the respondents had no vested right to the relief claimed and that the authorities were under no legal duty to grant it without observing the requirements of law. In the same vein, “Islamic Republic of Pakistan v. Muhammad Saeed”2 holds that one who seeks the performance of a public duty by mandamus must show a particular ground for claiming it, distinct from the general interest he shares with other members of the public. It follows that the writ enforces a duty which the law imposes in imperative terms. Where the law vests discretion in an authority, the Court may require that the 1 2005 SCMR 534 2 PLD 1961 SC 192 discretion be exercised, but it will not dictate the manner of its exercise or the conclusion to be reached, for that would be to substitute the judgment of the Court for that of the authority chosen by the legislature. The remedy is, moreover, discretionary and not a writ of course. It is ordinarily declined where an adequate alternate remedy exists or where the factual controversy is seriously disputed, as held in “Secretary to Government of the Punjab v. Ghulam Nabi”3.

Equally relevant to the controversy is the statutory framework within which the FIA acts upon a complaint of custodial torture. Such complaints are governed by the Torture and Custodial Death (Prevention and Punishment) Act, 2022 (“Act of 2022”), a law born of Pakistan’s obligations under the United Nations Convention against Torture and of the dignity of man guaranteed by Article 14 of the Constitution. Under Sections 2(1)(a) and (c), a “complaint” means allegations made orally or in writing to the FIA. Section 5(1) confers on the FIA, notwithstanding anything in any other law, exclusive jurisdiction to investigate complaints against public officials accused of offences under the Act, under the supervision of the National Commission for Human Rights. The legislative choice is deliberate. Allegations of torture against the police are entrusted to an agency other than the police, and its work is overseen by an independent commission, so that the inquiry into the conduct of public officials is not left to their own department. Section 5(2) requires a Magistrate who has reason to believe that such an offence has been committed, or before whom a person in custody complains of torture, to order a medical examination and, if it reveals torture, to notify the FIA. Section 5(3) provides that the FIA shall have the same powers and follow the same procedure as are prescribed in the Federal Investigation Agency Act, 1974 and the rules made thereunder. Offences under the Act are triable exclusively by the Court of Sessions under Section 6, and the provisions of the Cr.P.C. apply to proceedings under the Act save as otherwise provided.

It is in this statutory setting that the procedural regime of the FIA falls to be understood. The FIA is a specialised statutory agency, 3 PLD 2001 SC 415 established for the inquiry into and investigation of the offences entrusted to it by law, as explained in “F.I.A. through Director General, FIA and others v. Syed Hamid Ali Shah and others”4. By force of Section 5(3) of the Act of 2022, the Federal Investigation Agency (Inquiries and Investigations) Rules, 2002 (“Rules of 2002”) stand incorporated into its scheme. Rule 5(2) requires the prior permission of a designated authority, graded according to the pay scale of the accused public servant, before a criminal case is registered against him. Rule 5(4) obliges that authority to record its reasons where it declines to register a case. When these Rules are read together with Section 5(1), which speaks only of “investigation”, and Section 16, which gives the Act overriding effect, these provisions yield a scheme distinct from the general law. A complaint of custodial torture is not dealt with under Section 154 Cr.P.C. by an officer in charge of a police station. It is taken up by the FIA, and the registration of a case follows the decision of the designated authority under the Rules. That decision is not a matter of unfettered choice. It must rest on recorded reasons and is amenable to judicial review, as this Court has had occasion to observe in “Zubaida Qureshi v. Ex-Officio Justice of Peace and others”5. The scheme thus strikes a careful balance between two competing concerns. On the one hand, it protects the complainant against an arbitrary refusal to register a case; on the other, it shields public officials from the registration of a case against them without prior scrutiny by a responsible authority.

Turning next to the jurisdiction of the learned Ex-Officio Justice of the Peace, Section 22-A(6) Cr.P.C. empowers him to issue appropriate directions to the police authorities on complaints regarding, inter alia, the non-registration of a criminal case. The FIA, being a police force for these purposes, is equally amenable to that jurisdiction, as held in “Munir Ahmad Bhatti v. Director, FIA Cyber Crime Wing, Lahore and others”6. In “Younas Abbas and others v. Additional Sessions Judge, Chakwal and others”7, the Honourable Supreme Court 4 PLD 2023 SC 265 5 2024 LHC 3636 6 PLD 2022 Lahore 664 7 PLD 2016 SC 581 of Pakistan authoritatively enunciated that the functions performed under Section 22-A(6) are quasi-judicial, and not ministerial or administrative, in character. The Ex-Officio Justice of the Peace is, therefore, neither an automated conduit nor a post office, bound to direct registration of a case upon the mere presentation of an application alleging a cognizable offence. He is expected to decide upon an informed and judicious consideration of the matter before him. He is not obliged to call for a report in every case, but where he does, the report must receive proper consideration, as Honourable Full Bench of this Court held in “Khizer Hayat and others v. Inspector-General of Police (Punjab), Lahore and others”8 . Such a report may ascertain foundational facts, such as whether a case on the same occurrence is already registered, whether cross-versions have been recorded, or whether the matter is already seized by a specialised statutory agency such as the FIA. It cannot, however, be permitted to become a vehicle for a roving inquiry into the truth or falsity of the allegations, which remains the exclusive preserve of the investigating agency and, ultimately, of the trial court.

In the light of the jurisprudence expounded above, the first question presents no difficulty. The impugned order was passed in proceedings for compliance with the order dated 11.10.2025, and such proceedings are, by their very nature, confined to the four corners of the order sought to be complied with. Their purpose is to secure compliance of an order, not to reopen it. Were it otherwise, every compliance petition would become a second round of litigation on the merits, and the finality which the law attaches to an unchallenged order would be rendered illusory. The order dated 11.10.2025 directed the FIA to conclude an “inquiry” on merits within thirty days. It neither required the FIA to register a case nor to reach any particular conclusion. If the petitioner considered that the matter called for a direct investigation rather than an inquiry, the proper course was to challenge that order. He did not do so. Instead, he accepted it, appeared in the 8 PLD 2005 Lahore 470 inquiry, produced his evidence, and allowed the order to attain finality. Having elected that course, he cannot, in proceedings brought to enforce that very order, turn round and contend that the course it prescribed was impermissible. When the FIA reported that the inquiry had been concluded and dropped, the order stood complied with, and the learned Ex-Officio Justice of the Peace could neither enlarge its terms nor sit in appeal over the decision of the FIA. The impugned order is, therefore, neither illegal nor without lawful authority.

Quite apart from the above, the prayer for a writ of mandamus against the FIA stands on no firmer footing. As noticed in paragraph 8, the law does not impose on the FIA an unconditional duty to register a case upon every complaint. It requires the designated authority to evaluate the material and decide whether a case should be registered. A decision of that kind involves judgment, and it is precisely the kind of decision which mandamus cannot dictate. To direct the FIA to register a case would be to substitute the Court’s assessment of the material for that of the authority to which the legislature has entrusted it. The safeguards of recorded reasons and judicial review attach to the decision of that authority. That decision, however, is not before this Court. It is not the order impugned, and the petition was not framed as a challenge to it, so its reasons, or the want of them, cannot be examined here. Nor has the petitioner shown that the closure was without jurisdiction, “coram non judice or mala fide”. He merely reiterates his own version of the occurrence. Even where a want of reasons is established, the appropriate consequence is ordinarily a direction to reconsider the matter in accordance with law, not a writ directing the registration of a case.

Nor does the Medico Legal Examination Certificate carry the petitioner’s case any further. A Medico Legal Examination Certificate, particularly one founded on an examination conducted after some delay, may establish the existence of injuries. It does not, by itself, establish who caused them, the circumstances in which they were caused, or the involvement of the police officials named. Those questions, together with the alleged abduction and detention, are disputed questions of fact. They can only be answered by recording evidence, testing it in cross-examination and weighing it, which this Court does not undertake in constitutional jurisdiction, as held in Ghulam Nabi (supra). The law, however, provides a forum where precisely that can be done. The petitioner may file a private complaint before the court of competent jurisdiction, which, for offences under the Act of 2022, is the Court of Sessions under Section 6. That court can record his evidence, including the Medico Legal Examination Certificate, and summon the accused if a case is made out. The remedy is therefore not merely available but better suited to the controversy than the writ jurisdiction of this Court, which cannot be invoked to bypass it.

The upshot of the above discussion is that the impugned order dated 04.02.2026 suffers from no illegality, perversity or jurisdictional defect warranting interference in the exercise of constitutional jurisdiction, and no case is made out for a writ of mandamus against the FIA. The instant petition, being devoid of merit, is accordingly dismissed. The petitioner shall, however, be at liberty to file a private complaint before the court of competent jurisdiction, which, if filed, shall be decided on its own merits strictly in accordance with law, uninfluenced by any observation made herein or by the closure of the FIA inquiry. (MUHAMMAD JAWAD ZAFAR) JUDGE Approved for reporting Judge Gulfam/*
